intro: Patrizia Prati plays Chopin’s F♯-major Nocturne in the empty rooms of Madrid’s Museum of Romanticism. Its poised opening melody has a quick, murmuring double life in the middle.

sections.label: A · A singing line in F♯
sections.mNote: The melody curls above a gently moving left hand

sections.label: B · The quick, hushed middle
sections.mNote: Dotted rhythms and leaping bass, marked doppio movimento

sections.label: C · The first tune again
sections.mNote: A pause prepares the return of the slow melody

sections.label: D · The F♯-major close
sections.mNote: Small notes descend above the final bass

cues.title: An upbeat takes flight
cues.text: Two quick notes, A♯ and B, set the melody moving. The phrase falls, rests on repeated C♯s, then sends a flourish upwards. Chopin keeps adding new little runs to a tune that remains easy to recognise.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, upbeat and bars 1–16. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Chopin in a Madrid museum
cues.text: Prati records at the Museum of Romanticism on 24 November 2015, without an audience: a first concert there had been ruined by coughing and mobile phones. She gives the recordings to Wikimedia Spain, twelve Chopin nocturnes among them.
cues.evidence: Rubén Ojeda (Wikimedia España), “La música del Romanticismo suena en Wikipedia”, 14 February 2016: https://diff.wikimedia.org/es/2016/02/14/la-musica-del-romanticismo-suena-en-wikipedia/ ; Commons file page: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fryderyk_Chopin_-_Nocturne_op._15_n.2_Fis-dur_-_Patrizia_Prati.ogg

cues.title: Dotted notes over C♯
cues.text: The quick middle begins over a C♯ bass. The right hand is suddenly crowded: a dotted melody above a running accompaniment, both played sotto voce. The bass makes wide jumps while the tune grows more insistent.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 25–32: C♯ dominant harmony, doppio movimento and sotto voce. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A familiar upbeat
cues.text: The middle ends in repeated figures that slow and die away. A pause separates them from the returning A♯–B upbeat. The song comes back in the first tempo, still growing fresh ornaments.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 47–52, marked molto rallentando, smorzando and a Tempo. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A quiet tumble home
cues.text: The closing flourishes tumble down through the notes of F♯ major. Smorzando asks the piano to die away. At the bottom of all that decoration sits the last low F♯.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 60–62. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
